name: Uma Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I lead a team of nine claims handlers at a big insurance company, home and contents claims mostly. I'm in by half eight, I check the queue, I sign off anything over the limit my team can approve, and then it's meetings and fires. The bit I love is when someone's kitchen has flooded and my team gets them paid in a week instead of a month.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The targets that change every quarter, and the new systems head office keeps pushing on us. I'm not a gadget person, and I've never used one of those AI chat tools. I still keep a paper notebook for my one-to-ones, and Grace, my most senior handler, teases me about it every Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely. At work I'd say the people on my team were never the problem, and the money spent on AI pilots could have hired two more handlers. I don't really post online, but I'd share something from the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't feel safe. Our department has had two restructures in three years, and that had nothing to do with AI. Rent on the flat Theo and I share went up again in September, so even a normal year feels tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and push to get the two vacancies on my team filled. I'd join the staff union properly instead of just reading the emails, because the next restructure is coming anyway. And I'd put about a hundred more aside each month, because four months of savings isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, with a low hum of worry underneath. The worry was there before anyone said the word AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the next restructure is coming anyway. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every January a consultant turns up with a slide deck about efficiency. Last time they merged two claims teams and three people I liked took voluntary redundancy. Even if AI does nothing, the company will still find a slide that says we cost too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Kemal, he's the newest and he's on a fixed-term contract. He's good, but when they cut, they cut the contracts first. I'd tell him to get his name down for the permanent posts early.

say: My team was **never the problem**; the AI money should have paid for two more handlers.
I'd share the **union's posts** about protecting claims jobs, but I wouldn't write much myself.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but not safe, because restructures happen with or without AI.
The **rent rise** in September already makes a normal year feel tight.
do: Push head office to fill the **two vacancies** on my team.
Join the **staff union** properly instead of just reading its emails.
Save about **a hundred more** each month on top of current savings.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with a **low hum** of worry that was there before AI.
S0.quote: Even if AI does nothing, the company will still find a slide that says we cost too much.
fieldNote: Her worry is about **restructures** and cost-cutting, not technology, and it predates the AI question.
Strong **union** instinct shows up even in the mildest picture.
She is confident in her team's skills but distrusts **head office** decisions.

steps.text: Ask head office to fill the two open claims handler posts
Sign up as a full member of the staff union
Move an extra hundred a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper agreement before any of it touches claims, written down, with the union in the room. Online I'd share articles about companies that cut staff and then got buried in complaints. Claims is about judgement and people, not just ticking boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, checking and answering customers is half of what my team does. If software reads the photos and drafts the letters, head office will say I need four handlers, not nine. And then someone asks why four people need a team leader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a union rep on the rollout group, and I'd ask HR in writing what happens to roles that shrink. I'd cut back now, no holiday next summer, and keep that money as a cushion. And I'd quietly look at jobs in the council's housing repairs team, because that's still people work and it's public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would you learn them if it meant keeping your role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training if it was compulsory, I'm not daft about it. But I wouldn't volunteer to build the thing that replaces Grace. Grace has done this for nineteen years and can spot a dodgy claim from the first sentence of a phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner the night you heard the team was shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Theo I'm not going to wait for them to decide for me. He's a nurse, so his job is solid, and that helps. But I'd also say I don't want to be the one person on his ward's salary and nothing else.

say: We need a **written agreement** with the union before AI touches claims.
Claims work is about **judgement and people**, not just ticking boxes.
think: **Checking and answering** customers is half my team's work, so nine handlers could become four.
A smaller team makes my own **team leader role** easy to cut.
do: Ask for a **union rep** on the rollout group and ask HR in writing about shrinking roles.
Skip next summer's **holiday** and keep that money as savings.
Look quietly at **council jobs** in housing repairs.
feel: **Tense**, like waiting for a letter she knows is coming.
S1.quote: If software reads the photos and drafts the letters, head office will say I need four handlers, not nine.
fieldNote: She sees that her team's **core tasks** are on the list, and that her role follows the team.
Her resistance is about **loyalty** to colleagues like Grace as much as about technology.
Her partner's **nursing job** is a comfort, but she refuses to lean on it.

steps.text: Ask HR in writing what happens to claims roles that shrink
Cancel next summer's holiday and bank the money instead
Apply for council housing repairs coordinator jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need governments to step in, now, not after. Publicly I'd be angry, sharing every petition about protecting workers and taxing the companies that profit. At work I'd say out loud what everyone's thinking, which is that the whole floor is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is finished within the two years. Everything we do is reading, judging and writing, and that's the first thing it takes. The only bit left would be the loss adjusters who go out to the houses, and even that only lasts until the robots come three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food, straight away, and try to stretch four months of savings to six. I'd apply for council and hospital admin jobs before everyone else does, even at lower pay. I'd go to every union meeting and push for redundancy terms that actually mean something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, the kind where you wake up at four and do sums in your head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to move into the hands-on side, like loss adjusting, to buy those extra three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. A loss adjuster is still out in people's homes with a tape measure, and the robots come three years after the thinking part. But it's a different qualification, and I'd be starting at the bottom at twenty-eight with half the company trying to do the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the people at the top who'll make a fortune from it, and the governments who let it happen without rules. Not the technology itself. Not my team, and not the people who use it because they have to.

say: Governments must **step in now**, with protections and taxes on companies that profit.
I'd say at work that the **whole floor** is gone.
think: My job is **finished** within two years because it is all reading, judging and writing.
Only the **hands-on** loss adjusters last longer, until robots come three years later.
do: Stop all spending except **rent and food** to stretch savings to six months.
Apply for **council and hospital** admin jobs immediately, even at lower pay.
Push at **union meetings** for real redundancy terms.
feel: **Properly scared**, waking at four and doing sums in her head.
S2.quote: Everything we do is reading, judging and writing, and that's the first thing it takes.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright and says so without hedging.
Sees the **three-year gap** for hands-on work but doubts she can cross into it in time.
Blames **owners and governments**, explicitly not the technology or her colleagues.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food to stretch savings
Apply for council and hospital admin posts before the rush
Push the union for proper redundancy pay terms
Sign petitions for worker protection and taxes on AI profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them, and I'd mean the unions and the government as much as myself. I'd be louder online than usual, which isn't saying much. At work I'd ask head office for a plan, in writing, every single quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side of my job goes by 2031, I've no doubts about that. Five years means I'd be thirty-two, still renting, maybe thinking about kids with Theo. So it's not doom, but it's a clock on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time course in something hands-on or caring, probably a care coordinator qualification through the council. I'd save hard, about two hundred a month, to get the cushion to six months. And I'd stay at the insurer while it lasts, because the pay is decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less panic than the two-year one, but it sits on your chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change your plans with Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think we'd put it off. Theo wants kids by thirty, and I keep saying let's see where my job is. Under this picture I'd want a second income sorted before we try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to learn the new tools. Why not go that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning the AI tools wouldn't save the job, it would just make me better at running the thing that replaces us. I'd rather put the hours into a skill that still needs a person in the room, like care.

say: We have **five years**, so unions and government must use them too.
I'd ask head office for a **written plan** every quarter.
think: The **thinking side** of my job is gone by 2031.
At thirty-two I'd still be **renting**, so it's a clock on the wall, not doom.
do: Start a **part-time course** in care coordination through the council.
Save about **two hundred** a month to reach six months of cushion.
Stay at the insurer while the **pay** lasts.
feel: **Heavy** rather than panicked; it sits on her chest.
S3.quote: Learning the AI tools wouldn't save the job, it would just make me better at running the thing that replaces us.
fieldNote: Still expects to **lose the job**; extra time changes her plans, not the outcome.
Chooses **care work** over learning AI, consistent with her resistance and values.
AI is reshaping **family plans**: children now wait on a second income.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time council care coordinator course
Put two hundred a month into savings until six months saved
Hold off on trying for children until a second income is sorted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we let companies decide everything. I'd push for training money and proper rules at work and online. I'd probably be one of those people who emails her local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it something I can plan around. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, with time to have moved into something more human. I'd still lose this job, I think, but I wouldn't lose my footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the care coordinator course in the second or third year, not right away, once I see which way it's going. I'd keep saving steadily and keep the union membership. I'd ask about moving onto the complex claims team, where there's more phone work with vulnerable customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but I can breathe. It feels like a long winter forecast, not a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're starting later in this picture than the five-year one. Is that your slowness with change talking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, yes. I've always taken my time with change. But this one is different, because if I wait till year eight, everyone else in insurance will be queuing for the same courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, mostly. She's fifty-three, and ten years takes her right to the edge of retirement but not over it. I'd want the union to fight for her to go out on her own terms.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if used well, and a waste if companies decide everything.
I'd push for **training money** and rules, and email my local councillor.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd have time to move into something more human.
I'd still **lose this job**, but I wouldn't lose my footing.
do: Start the **care coordinator** course in year two or three.
Ask to move onto the **complex claims** team with more phone work.
Keep **saving steadily** and keep the union membership.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, like a long winter forecast.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift if we use it, and a waste if we let companies decide everything.
fieldNote: Extra time softens her tone but she still expects to **lose this job** eventually.
Admits her **slowness** with change and sees the risk of everyone queuing for retraining.
Her concern for **older colleagues** like Grace is constant across scenarios.

steps.text: Ask to transfer onto the complex claims phone team
Begin the care coordinator course in the second or third year
Email the local councillor about AI retraining money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no contest. There's no time to retrain, and everyone in my building would be job hunting in the same month. What would help is redundancy pay that's actually decent, and free retraining for care and public service jobs that pays you while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets to decide. Nobody asked my team if they wanted this, and nobody will. I think a lot of people my age would feel better if workers had an actual seat when these things are rolled out.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked my team if they wanted this, and nobody will.
portrait: Uma, 27, leads **nine claims handlers** at a large insurer and rents a flat with her partner Theo, a nurse.
She has never used AI tools and is wary of **head office** systems and restructures.
Her outlook is **pro-union** and she blames owners and governments, not technology or colleagues.
She moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to alarmed when AGI arrives in two or five years.
Her answer to change is **care work** and union pressure, not learning the tools that replace her team.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because everyone in her building would be **job hunting** at once.
whatWouldHelp: Decent **redundancy pay** and paid retraining for care and public service jobs.
Giving workers **a seat** when AI is rolled out.
